new_statements.quote: Known varieties of Uab Meto have the five vowels /i e a o u/.7 Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel. Vowel-initial words begin with a predictable glottal stop; /asu/ ‘dog’ → [ˈʔasʊ]. While all Uab Meto varieties appear to share the same phoneme inventory, the segments in each variety have different distributions and behaviors.

new_statements.relation_note: Catalog penultimate stress is penultimate stress; Edwards states word stress on the penultimate vowel for all known Uab Meto varieties, whose Amarasi data are Kotos Amarasi (Nekmese', Koro'oto hamlet) and Ro'is Amarasi (Buraen, Suit hamlet). new_statements.rule_in_words: Word stress falls on the penultimate vowel in all known Uab Meto varieties, Amarasi (Kotos and Ro'is) included; the example /asu/ 'dog' is [ˈʔasʊ]. The paper is a historical-phonology study and has no dedicated stress or prosody section; this one sentence in the phoneme-inventory overview is its only statement on stress.
new_statements.exceptions: None mentioned. The only other uses of 'penultimate' in the paper (p. 63, PMP *e > e in penultimate syllables) concern historical vowel reflexes, not stress.
new_statements.identity_note: Edwards 2016 (OL) makes its stress statement for 'known varieties of Uab Meto' as a whole, not for Amarasi specifically; its Amarasi data are Kotos Amarasi (village Nekmese', hamlet Koro'oto, ~1,600-headword dictionary and 2.5 h of texts) and Ro'is Amarasi (village Buraen, hamlet Suit), plus Molo (Middelkoop's draft dictionary) and occasional Amfo'an, Kusa-Manea, Baikeno and Amanuban data. Amarasi is one variety of the Uab Meto cluster covered by the blanket statement.

tone_statements.citation: Edwards, Owen. 2020. Metathesis and unmetathesis in Amarasi (Studies in Diversity Linguistics 29). Berlin: Language Science Press. doi:10.5281/zenodo.3700413
tone_statements.quote: p.111: "Stress in Amarasi falls on the penultimate syllable of the prosodic word. ... The three main correlates of stress in Amarasi are duration, pitch, and intensity. A stressed vowel is typically realised with higher pitch, increased intensity, and is longer when compared to unstressed vowels." p.192: "Based on preliminary data on a north-eastern variety of Meto, McConvell & Kolo (1996) raise the possibility that metathesis in Meto could be prosodically conditioned. They noted that they had two examples of a U-form verb with falling or low pitch, and two examples of an M-form verb with rising or high pitch."

sources.quote: 'Finally, when the second vowel of words with the structure (C)VVCV(C) is a high vowel, it is universally realised as a glide. In such words the antepenultimate vowel is also the locus of stress placement rather than the usual penultimate vowel. An example is /aikaʔ/ thorn -> [ˈʔajkɐʔ].' Also p. 122: pronouns 'are often unstressed'; vowel-sequence off-gliding more frequent 'when the vowel sequence does not bear phrasal stress'.

sources.note: No tone: pitch is treated only as one of three phonetic correlates of penultimate stress (higher pitch on the stressed vowel, p.111, with measurements in Table 3.9); sec. 4.4.2.1 tests McConvell & Kolo's (1996) suggestion that Meto U-forms vs M-forms differ in pitch (falling/low vs rising/high) on 160 verbs from texts and finds 'the pitch of both U-form and M-form verbs is very similar' (Table 4.12). No lexical or grammatical tone posited.

tone.quote: Amarasi words have a highly restricted phonotactic structure. Content words (as opposed to grammatical functors) are minimally composed of a disyllabic foot that is maximally CV(C)V(C). This foot can be optionally preceded by another consonant, another syllable, or another foot. Stress falls on the penultimate syllable of the foot, with secondary stress on every second syllable to the left.
